patent: Filed 1945-10-08 and issued 1950-01-24 to Percy L. Spencer, assignor to Raytheon Manufacturing Company. It claims cooking food with microwave energy: wavelength in the microwave region (claims 1-3) or of substantially ten centimeters, about 3 GHz (claims 4-6), confined and guided to a region where the food is exposed, optionally while a conveyor moves it through. The stated rationale is that a wavelength comparable to the size of the food heats it far more efficiently than the earlier radio-frequency heating at up to 50 megacycles. The source is a pair of cavity magnetrons, the tube Raytheon mass-produced for radar during the Second World War. Raytheon sold the first commercial microwave oven, the Radarange, from 1947. Domestic ovens later settled on 2.45 GHz, about 12.2 cm in free space.

figs.1: The whole apparatus in one schematic. Magnetrons 10 (top) and 11 (bottom) are circles with eight radial anode vanes 13 around a small central cathode 14. Envelopes 12 go to the two ends of transformer secondary 17 by conductors 15 and 16; the cathodes are joined by 20 and 21 and returned to the secondary's center tap by 22 (the dots are junctions), so each tube conducts on alternate half-cycles of the 60-cycle supply. Each tube's output is picked up by a loop (26, 27) in one vane cavity and carried by coaxial line 24 or 25, drawn as a tube, into the closed left end of wave guide 23; the guide is broken away near its open outlet to show its wall in section. The food sits on the hatched belt over roller 28 just beyond the outlet. The boxed captions are drawing labels only.

parts.12: The copper envelope is also the anode block; the vanes 13 project inward from it.
parts.26: Drawn as a small hook in the cavity beside the top vane of magnetron 10, where line 24 ends; loop 27 sits likewise beside the bottom vane of magnetron 11.
parts.28: The numeral's arrow points to the roller; the CONVEYOR SYSTEM caption points to the belt carrying the food.

glossary.def: A vacuum tube oscillator in which electrons from a central cathode, bent by a magnetic field along the tube axis, drive resonant cavities in the surrounding anode block. The cavity magnetron generates kilowatts at centimetre wavelengths.
A closed metal space that resonates at frequencies set by its dimensions; here each gap between adjacent vanes with the envelope behind it.

Two devices driven in antiphase. Here the anodes sit at opposite ends of the secondary with the cathodes at its center tap, so the tubes conduct on alternate half-cycles and the transformer needs no separate rectifier.
A connection to the midpoint of a transformer winding.
Unrectified alternating current straight from the supply.
Release of electrons from a heated cathode; an alkaline-earth oxide coating (barium, strontium, calcium oxides) emits strongly at moderate temperature.
A centre conductor inside a tubular outer conductor, carrying radio-frequency power with the field confined between them.
A small wire loop in a resonator that links its magnetic field and feeds the energy into a transmission line.
A hollow metal pipe that carries microwaves as fields inside it; it passes only wavelengths shorter than about twice its wider internal dimension.
